Meta Investment Memo: Pumping AI Iron It’s still January which means gyms are full of new year resolutioners, weather permitting. In the AI gym, where gains are measured in tokens and MMLU scores, Meta looks the scrawny kid in a gym full of bodybuilders named Claude, Gemini, GPT, and Grok. But don’t mistake size for strength. What if Meta is the elite bodybuilder Anatoly in disguise? And isn’t the point to get in shape, not just look bigger? It’s an expensive gym membership, but “the greatest feeling you can get is the pump” . Expect Meta to still be lifting in December. The frontier model barbell. If Meta’s new model scores at or near peers, amazing. And if model performance falls well short with no path to close the gap, Meta can wind down investment and partner (see: Apple). The most likely and feared outcome, however, is the middle where Meta’s new model lands “close but not quite, ” driving another step up in investment with no guarantees they can catch the pack - this outcome is still favorable if... … Meta can get in shape. Model performance KPIs have anointed AI winners and losers for now, but AI product adoption and monetization matter more than another basis point improvement on some LLM test. On this front, Meta’s productization capability may be second to none. The company can ship products at scale across their owned channels, and we expect a barrage of shipments this year — remember, Meta AI counts 1B+ monthly users powered by an average model - what if the next model is good? An expensive gym but contract locked in? The ‘significant’ step up in expenses to cover AI talent, compute, and depreciation flow through is worrisome if it’s too high or returns remain uncertain. But there’s no terminal risk. Any indication around peak investment intensity should drive upward revisions and stock re-rating - exactly what’s needed to retain AI talent. Investment Implications Backing the scrawny kid to flex their muscle in 2026. Remain Outperform PT $870. DETAILS
THE 2026 META SET UP - LLAMA, LLAMA, META DRAMA
2025 was perhaps the most violent, temperamental, and emotional market we’ve seen in quite a while. From DeepSeek to
T ariffs to OpenAI (not covered) news flow pixie dust turned poison saw us crowning AI winners and losers simultaneously
resulting in high torque stock swings. The commonality? Underwriting the unknowable. We’re all well aware that the market in
the near-term is a voting machine, but even still we’ve had more than a few senior PM and CIOs acknowledge that 2025 may
have been their hardest year in the seat.
Perhaps no better stock exemplifies this Market’s finickiness than Meta. Over the past 6 months, we’ve seen a ~15-turn
swing between Meta and Google’s Forward PE multiples. 15x T urns! How do we explain that?
Give Google credit. Of course some of that is warranted as Google managed to capture a regulatory clearing event, Gemini
model success and usage acceleration, TPU enterprise traction, and solid search performance all compressed in this 6-month
window. Google also found themselves as the antidote to numerous thematics: Convinced AI is a bubble? Head to Google.
Believe in AI but not in the OpenAI complex? Google again. And if you simply ignore the AI debate but acknowledge a strong ad
market with more ad dollars coming from publishers needing traffic, Google continues to deliver on search revenues. But this
memo is not about Google.
From ‘AI winner’ to ‘AI winner for core’ . From mid-2024, Meta was a consensus AI winner. ChatGPT wasn’t coming after
social, and if anyone could take advantage of AI for ad targeting, measurement, and creative… well that was Meta in a nutshell.
And Meta absolutely delivered with AI-powered efforts including Lattice, GEM, and Andromeda on the ad delivery side and
unifying the content recommendation algorithm across surfaces drove accelerating levels of ad revenues and engagement we
no longer thought possible for a company of Meta’s size. Some of our previous estimates suggest that Meta could be seeing a
20-25% ROIC on AI investments going towards core products.
Revenue growth not a top-3 debate. For as long as we’ve been covering Meta, there’s always been some flavor of a revenue
or engagement metric that was the singular KPI on the stock. We don’t expect this lull to last too long as there’s still room to
debate what inning we’re in on the laundry list of AI-driven improvements and whether the return of TikT ok, entry of ChatGPT
into the ad space, and changes to European operations could impact ad market share. Most investors we speak with feel
comfortable in the ad growth story which remains the primary reason to own the stock here.
No obvious terminal risk from Gen AI disruption. Amazingly, Meta’s de-rating occurred right when revenue growth
accelerated to levels thought no longer attainable - growth went up 10ppts from 16% Y/Y reported in 1Q25 to 26% Y/
Y for 3Q25, and investors appear comfortable with a high-teens to 20%+ growth for 2026 and beyond in a stable macro
environment vs. the low-to-mid teens prior consensus range. Meta remains the clearest example of AI-delivered returns
powering improved ad delivery/targeting and more personalized content recommendations - exactly what the bull case was in
mid 2024!
Frontier lab = Metaverse PTSD? If ad revenue growth was that all that mattered we’d struggle to explain why Meta’s stock
drew down ~15-20% post 3Q25 earnings. However, management’s comments emphasized that the company is all-in on
bringing a frontier model to market backed by ‘significantly’ accelerating investment levels. Given the step-up in CapEx and
OpEx are strategic with uncertain ROIC, it’s understandable that investors with long memories of the Metaverse build out are
worried we are once again embarking on a similar journey into the unknown.
• Does Meta need a frontier model? Even if the Llama program was more successful, we’ve often been asked why Meta
doesn’t simply partner with a frontier model builder rather than enter into this arms race with no obvious cloud compute or
enterprise business to fall back on. Indeed, Meta does use Midjourney for some of their AI Image Generation capabilities
and if one believes Meta’s real competitive advantages is owning the attention of 3.5B daily consumers, then why not follow
Apple which recently entered into a partnership with Google for Gemini to power Siri? The house view is that owning a model
allows the company to ship product faster, which may well be true, and if the model is sourced from a competitor there may
come a point where their partner self-preferences their own offering. Indeed, Meta’s rocky relationship with landlords like
Apple (in-app apps, IDFA, payments) are well documented (Apple is covered by Mark Newman).
• What went wrong with Llama? We’re not exactly sure beyond delays to Llama 4’s Behemoth model and rumblings that the
model was over-fitted to score well on LLM rankings. It wasn’t a bad model, but it also wasn’t keeping pace with performance

from other frontier labs. For the sports fans, it reminds us of a perennial playoff team that can never quite get over the hump
and decides to finally swap out their coach/manager and trade for big talent (the Golden State Warriors would be a great
outcome and hopefully our Buffalo Bills follow). Meta’s high-profile $15B acquisition of ScaleAI and well publicized high
price tag offers for AI talent and associated compute needs was a self admission that the Llama program had hit a wall and
needed a reset.
• A binary call on Avocado. After massive personnel and org hierarchy changes to the AI team under a new Superintelligence
Labs (MSL) unit, investors remain in a holding pattern waiting to see whether the company’s new frontier models are at or
close to current leading models:
• Delicious guacamole: If Avocado - the reported name of Meta’s latest LLM - is competitive, the overhang likely
dissipates, and we can put Meta back into the ‘AI winner’ cohort. After all, a great model followed by product shipments
that push the model across 3.5B daily users is much easier to underwrite (see: Google 2025).
• Head to Chipotle: If the avocado model is so far behind that it’s inconceivable Meta can ever catch the frontier, Zuck will
have a complex decision to make. But if the data truly shows no chance of catching the lead pack, we believe rationality
will prevail and Meta retains a decent get-out-of-jail free card that would appeal to investors - wind down investment
levels and partner with a third-party LLM. While fears of partnering with a competitor such as Google or OpenAI are
valid, we’d offer Anthropic (private) as an ideal partner that has so far shown little appetite to go after consumer (Chipotle
covered by Danilo Gargiulo).
• Some brown spots (most likely): If the model is close but not quite, questions around (a) whether sustained or elevated
investment levels can close the model quality gap, and (b) how long would Meta prolong the investment cycle and
impairment to longer-term FCF/EPS questions get louder. We suspect signals of being behind have a greater impact of
stock performance than actual model benchmarks, though investment burn-rate is real. While LLM benchmarks matter,
product matters more and Meta remains well positioned here. Even with a ‘lagging’ model, Meta still counts 1B+
Meta AI users.
FCF > everything. If investors start to question your place in the AI race, higher investments levels no longer get rewarded
but penalized. With Meta pointing to another ‘significant’ step up in capital and operating expenditures for 2026+, there’s a lot
more hesitancy to support an investment cycle with uncertainty around both returns and duration. Meta has proven sustained
AI-fueled high ROIC ad performance improvements, yet the investor worry here is whether all of that benefit will simply get reinvested into chasing ‘strategic’ model performance improvements. Suddenly, the 2026 FCF compression feels much harder to
underwrite.
• How significant is the significant step-up in expenses? The top debate we’ve had on Meta this year is around how
high can expenses go. Once you add in (1) the uptick in depreciation, (2) a full year of expensive AI resource-related costs
and expected hiring cadence, and (3) all the third-party cloud compute needs promised to the expensive AI hires until own
infrastructure is up and running, you can start to draw a line to $155B+ vs. Street closer to $150B. ~30%+ Y/Y expense
growth vs. the ~20% penciled in for revenue growth, and you can see the challenge facing investors here. Perhaps some
surgical cuts in other parts of the business such as reported cuts in non-AI reality labs team may offer some reprieve; is there
enough room to cut costs elsewhere to cap spending cadence?
• Is the CapEx really fungible? Management commentary that capital investment (also expected to grow another $35-40B
+ Y/Y) is going towards fungible hard assets - so not Metaverse 2.0 - has so far failed to remove the overhang. In particular,
soundbites around the ability to repurpose the compute if the frontier model bet doesn’t work out sound fair and practical in
theory. However in practice, it’s hard to articulate and define what the set of criteria needs to look like to trigger the fungibility
event - if Meta is close but not quite there in their frontier model efforts, do we see a fungibility event or further investment in
pursuit of the frontier?
THE META 2026 PITCH - NO MORE LLAMA DRAMA
Over the past five years, the annual performance gap between the best and worst Magnificent 7 stock has been 40%+. Simply
positioning correctly within the group generates meaningful alpha, and we see Meta as a relative winner within the group.
We think the debate around Meta’s model performance is the wrong one, and exactly why Meta is a stock worth
owning here. Ad revenues should continue to deliver aided by new surfaces as evidenced by the recent scale up of Threads
ads internationally, and strong ad spending tailwinds. Even if Meta’s new frontier model trails peers, its massive user base and

the company’s product-heavy DNA point to a robust slate of new product launches with strong monetization potential this year.
Investment levels are certainly elevated, but we expect that we’ll see evidence in 2026 around (1) digital ad TAM expansion with
AI creative and chatbot aided commercial activity, (2) progress on non-ad initiatives with a viral moment, and (3) a reminder of
cost discipline elsewhere in the business. If the company can point to 2026 as peak investment intensity with EPS and FCF
poised for acceleration in 2027+, the narrative and stock performance will follow… which is exactly what the company needs to
pay all that expensive AI talent.
Are we sure about the binary model outcome? Deliver a world-class model and Meta’s back to an AI winner; miss completely
and a ‘get out of jail’ third-party deal with a sharp pullback in investment levels likely sees investors reward the company
anyways. The most likely outcome - that the model is good but not quite as good as peers - worries investors that we’ll enter a
prolonged investment cycle with no guarantees on either returns or duration.
• Product traction > Model performance all day and twice on sundays. Maybe we’ve been consumer Internet analysts
too long, but the best technology doesn’t always win in the consumer realm. There’s a reason why adoption and engagement
KPIs tend to take priority when valuing consumer tech stocks. For example, which would you rather have? A company that
delivers a world-class model that ranks well but fails to drive any meaningful adoption (Grok may be closest here), or a decent
model followed by a slew of product shipments that go viral with an app hitting the top of the app stores and hockey-stick like
user growth? We prefer the latter camp, and this is exactly where we expect Meta to excel.
• A hefty AI-powered product slate for 2026? One of our key themes in 2026 is the ‘AI winner’ criteria shifts from model
performance → product usage and revenue generation. Part of what we believe has contributed to Google’s sustained stock
strength has been the consistent cadence of in-demand product shipments that have followed the Gemini 3 model release.
We suspect Meta has their own slate of product shipments ready to go once Avocado (and perhaps other models) is out the
door. As a nice tailwind to build upon, it sounds like pre-training for the new model went well (CTO speech at Davos), which
could move up the timeline for Avocado release to early spring vs. early summer base case.
Meta’s product DNA to expand into AI. Historically, Meta has repeatedly demonstrated their ability to develop and scale
new products including Reels (overtaking TikT ok), Threads (overtaking X), even MetaAI (1B+ monthly users) and the young but
supply-constrained wearables business. But it’s not just new products, it’s turbo-charging existing products with AI capabilities
such as folding new models into content recommendation and ad targeting; enhancing Advantage+, a $60B ARR franchise
now testing AI‑powered ad creative, and the continued push of enhancing WhatsApp’s adoption and business messaging
capabilities.
AI for everyone. We often find ourselves constrained by what is, that we miss what could be. Meta has numerous stakeholders
here worth considering: (1) users, (2) creators, (3) businesses, (4) advertisers, and (5) internal. Putting on our creative hats,
here’s what we think Meta could bring to market this year powered by AI:
• Turbo-charge core: Most obvious, but we don’t think we’re in the later innings here and there’s plenty more wood to chop to
drive up both engagement and advertiser ROI (Exhibit 7).
• AI Advantage+ creative & the return of Off-Meta ads (FAN): Democratizing customer acquisition has long been a goal of
Meta’s ad ambitions. Meta has already suggested that more of the ad tech can be automated away for their 10M+ advertisers
including personalizing ad creative powered by Mango (the reported name of the image/video LLM) to be most effective.
We’re in agreement with Sam Altman that Instagram ads are accretive to our experience, so what if Meta gets back into
helping advertisers not just run campaigns on Meta, but across other surfaces and apps as well?
• Meta AI 2.0... search ads: Yes, Meta already counts 1B+ monthly users, but we believe most of this usage is infrequent and/
or low monetization. With the enhancement from a better model, we could see a relaunch of the Meta AI standalone app.
Within Meta AI across apps, we expect to see Meta look to develop and monetize commercial search behavior as they too vie
for the personal assistant.
• Edits 2.0… Creator CGI: Meta Vibes was a fun test of AI-generated videos. But alongside Sora, the novelty of ‘AI-slop’
has faded. Instead, what if Meta enhanced the creator Edits application to include more AI content creation tools, think
CGI for creators. As a bonus, Meta has quietly offered a Meta Verified subscription for creators. What if Meta offered an AIpowered influencer enhancement subscription that helps design and deploy audience reach strategies to improve creator
monetization? What’s that worth?

• AI Business agents: We’ve long opined on the untapped potential of WhatsApp with Business Messaging already hitting a
$1B+ ARR. Beyond WhatsApp, there are 200M+ businesses with a presence on Meta, and newly powered by the Manus AI
acquisition, Meta can offer effective AI staffing or agents across customer support, sales, marketing, back-office, off-Meta
apps & websites, and anything else you can dream up. We do note that the Manus AI deal is currently been investigated by
Chinese regulators.
• Meta Shops 2.0: Analysts can dream can’t we? On paper, Facebook Shops had every right to win though we won’t get into
the autopsy of what happened here. If we really are entering the Age of Agents with new agentic shopping protocols from
OpenAI and Google already out the door, why couldn’t Meta follow suite given their breadth of consumer attention, existing
business relationships, and uncanny intent algorithms?
• Neural Band 2.0: Meta has sold 2M+ smart glasses, a good start but not quite needle moving just yet. As mentioned above
we expect the utility of the glasses to improve powered by a smarter Meta AI. And yet while glasses are the obvious play for
a media company like Meta, we found ourselves most impressed by the haptics capabilities contained in the Neural Band.
Given the Limitless acquisition (that records and tracks conversations), we’d propose a Neural Band-only product that can
listen & recall, toggle Meta AI with a tap, contain all the current Neural Ban capabilities, and integrate with our smartphones.
Could 2026 be peak investment intensity? Only Zuck knows. The recent “Meta Compute” AI infrastructure initiative sounds
profound with reports suggesting plans to bring ‘hundreds of gigawatts’ online overtime. We get this language may spook
investors, but at the end of the day you’re buying Meta because it’s a growth company which means a lot of bets won’t work
out. But as we’ve seen with the Media sector, eventually growth stalls out if all you’re fighting for is eyeballs. If “[Meta] doesn’t
build the things that disrupt Facebook, someone else will” . Reports of a recent reality lab RIF could reassure investors that
management understands the trade-off between going after long-term growth vs. near-term financial performance and
applying discipline to focus spend on high-priority areas. Are there more efficiencies to be found across Meta to self-fund
further AI needs?
Looking back in December 2026. This is really where we should be on Meta, though we understand why there’s such intense
focus on the 4Q print and investment guidance. We’ll paraphrase Susan Li’s paraphrasing of an investor question on a recent
podcast “why should investors buy the stock today and not just wait for the new thing to come out and buy the stock then?”
Expect investment guidance to tie to strong revenue trajectory. Overlay a new model launch, a laundry list of new products
to come, a pocket of new non-ad revenues picking up, and the narrative to turn once again as we start looking at EPS/FCF
reacceleration in 2027. Meta cares about their stock, so do we, and all the AI talent they’ve scooped up. Meta remains one of
our top picks for 2026 and could well see a story similar to Google 2025.
There are some near-term noises around core that we’d be remiss not to highlight given all the focus on AI and the model. Global
trends to age gate social media continue though we note Meta sees limited revenue contribution from younger users; The
European Commission’s ruling requiring Meta to offer alternatives to personalized ads could create a slight headwind to EU
revenues by our estimates; lastly the return of TikT ok and the launch of ChatGPT display ads may drive some ad budget shifts
though we again note that smaller, experimental ad budgets are more at risk in the near-term given Meta’s proven ROI track
record.
ESTIMATE AND PT REVISIONS
• Revenues: We take up FY 26 and FY27 revenue estimates to reflect higher confidence in continued user, engagement,
ad efficacy gains, ability to ramp monetization across broader surfaces, revenue from future AI products, and wearables
momentum.
• Margins: We take up our FY26 and FY27 total expense estimates to reflect management commentary.The growth in
expenses is mainly driven by the upwards revision in infrastructure operating costs, infrastructure investment which will
continue to flow through deprecation, and full-year compensation related charges tied to high-profile AI hires.
• EPS: We slightly take down our FY26 and FY27 EPS estimates due to the increased revenue growth and cost growth
roughly offsetting each other.
• CAPEX: We slightly take up our 2026 CapEx estimates to reflect Meta’s recent AI infrastructure & computing initiatives.
• We remain Outperform on Meta, with a PT of $870/share, implying 24x 2027E P/E. We value Meta using a 50/50
combination of 2027E EV/Sales multiple of 8x, and a DCF using an unchanged WACC of 10% and a terminal growth of

VALUATION METHODOLOGY
Meta Platforms Inc.
We value Meta on a Price T arget of $870 using a 50/50 combination of 2027e EV/Sales multiple of 8x, and a DCF using a WACC
of 9% and a terminal growth of 3.5%. We consider Meta primarily a digital advertising business and benchmark valuation to
comparable peers in this industry set.
Alphabet Inc
We value Alphabet on a Price T arget of $305, using a 50/50 combination of 2027e EV/ EBIT multiple of 23x and a DCF using
a WACC of 9% and a terminal growth of 3.0%. We consider Alphabet primarily a digital advertising business and benchmark
valuation to comparable peers in this industry set.
RISKS
Meta Platforms Inc.
Downside risk to our target price:
• Meta is currently under investigation in multiple regulatory proceedings now mostly focused on anti-trust domestically and
abroad.
• Signs that we’re reaching maturity in digital ads, increased competition as alternatives emerge with compelling ad ROIs, or further
privacy related changes (e.g., Cookie depreciation) could all put press on Meta's revenue outlook resulting in compressing revenue
growth and de-rating.
• Meta's metaverse aspirations could lead to margin headwinds and potentially minimal ROIC, which could negatively affect both
estimates and multiples.
Alphabet Inc
Upside risk to our price target:
• Faster than expected revenue growth tied to digital advertising recovery and idiosyncratic efforts or better than expected
margins tied to recent effort to slow down hiring and small scale lay-offs.
• Favorable regulatory outcomes further entrenching Google’s incumbency positions across both Search and Network.
Downside risk to our price target:
• T erminal risk narratives tied to Search disintermediation, either from negative headlines or share loss (users and/or revenue)
in search. If search were to suffer topline changes it could have a trickle effect across the business and have a material impact
on GOOGL 's ad revenues and we would expect further de-rating in the stock.
• Alphabet is currently under investigation in multiple regulatory proceedings across both anti-trust and privacy, domestically
and abroad. In particular, the DOJ case against Google on Search will likely reach a verdict later this year.
